note: Hebrew ketonet passim probably means a robe reaching to the palms and soles (pas = extremity), i.e. a long-sleeved, full-length garment; "many colours" follows the Septuagint's poikilos and is a guess. Also in vv. 23 and 32. Context: a long robe with sleeves (low confidence). Ketonet passim recurs only in 2 Sam 13:18-19, a princess's garment, so it marks status. Pas 'palm/sole' suggests a robe reaching to wrists and ankles, as Aquila, Symmachus and the LXX of 2 Sam 13:18 (karpotos) took it; but the LXX here and a proposed Akkadian parallel point to colour or ornament. The meaning is genuinely uncertain; confidence lowered. Other possible meanings: (1) 'a coat of many colours / multicolored tunic' — LXX chitona poikilon, Vulgate polymitam, KJV, ESV, NASB; (2) 'an ornate/ornamented robe' (embroidered or with appliqué) — NIV, NJPS, cf. Akkadian kitu pisannu; (3) 'a special tunic', leaving the feature unstated — NET; (4) a tunic of fine wool — Rashi.
Hebrew nekot and lot are aromatic gums (tragacanth and labdanum/ladanum); lot is not myrrh, which is mor in Hebrew.

kjv: go down into the grave unto my (Jacob's) son
mine: go down to my (Jacob's) son in Sheol
note: Hebrew she'olah is Sheol, the underworld abode of the dead; the KJV alternates between "grave", "hell" and "pit", which obscures that it is one consistent term.
The Masoretic text reads hammedanim (Medanites, cf. Medan in Gen 25:2); the KJV follows the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint and Vulgate, which harmonise with "Midianites" in v. 28.
